problem_statement: The paper frames the task as pricing European call options in a risk-neutral financial market. It presents the binomial tree as the classical option-pricing setup and proposes a quantum-walk-based version that can consider multiple possible asset-price states.
problem_statement_quotes: In this paper, we propose a quantum option pricing model in a risk-neutral framework.
In financial theory, the binomial tree pricing method is a widely used option pricing model, which uses random walk to model financial markets.
classical_baseline: The paper treats the classical binomial tree option pricing model of Cox, Ross, and Rubinstein as the baseline, and notes that in the limit of sufficiently small time steps it is consistent with the Black–Scholes model.
classical_baseline_quotes: In financial theory, the binomial tree pricing method is a widely used option pricing model, which uses random walk to model financial markets. J.C. Cox, R.A. Ross, and M. Rubinstein [11] first proposed the binomial tree option pricing method in their 1979 paper titled "Option Pricing: A Simplified Approach".
In the limit of sufficiently small time steps, this model is consistent with the Black–Scholes model [12].
Classical Binomial Tree Model: Based on Cox-Ross-Rubinstein’s Classical Binomial Tree Pricing Approach, which calculates option prices under risk-neutral assumptions;
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical one-step or two-step binomial tree gives only rough approximations, and that smaller time intervals are needed to get closer to the true option price. It also contrasts the classical model with its quantum version by saying the classical approach depends on assumed rise/fall probabilities, whereas the quantum model does not need those assumptions.
classical_difficulty_quotes: If it is assumed that price changes during the option’s lifetime are expressed only by a one-step or two-step binomial tree, then the option prices obtained will be very rough approximations.
The smaller the time intervals, the more stock price states are determined prior to the expiry date, and the closer the resulting option price estimate is to the true one.
It is evident that the binomial tree pricing in classical case depends on the assumption of the probability of stock price rises or falls.
Compared to the classical case, there is no need to assume the probabilities of the stock price rising or falling.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit and centered on option pricing; no strong real-world business stakes beyond pricing accuracy are stated.
